title: Periodic trends; Emission spectra and energy levels
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT02#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT02#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT02#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT02#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS03#N.3a, PT02#N.4a, AS03#N.6a, PT02#N.6, AS03#N.9, PT02#N.10, AS03#N.12, PT02#N.12, PT02#N.14.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Periodicity
items.clue: The pattern of trends repeating across each row of the table.

items.label: Shielding
items.clue: Inner electrons repel outer ones, reducing the pull they feel from the nucleus.

items.label: Isoelectronic
items.clue: Describes species such as O²⁻, F⁻ and Na⁺ that all share the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.

items.label: Electronegativity
items.clue: Ability of an atom to attract the shared pair in a covalent bond; fluorine is highest at 4.0.

questions.stem: When sodium compounds are heated in a flame, the flame turns yellow. Which process in the sodium atoms produces this yellow light?

options.text: Excited electrons fall to lower energy levels, emitting photons.
Electrons absorb energy and emit photons as they rise to higher levels.
Electrons escape from the atoms entirely, releasing energy as photons.
The hot atoms glow with the yellow colour that sodium atoms possess.

questions.explanation: Each fall emits a photon whose energy equals the gap between the levels; sodium's main gap gives yellow light.

questions.stem: The ions Na⁺, F⁻, Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ all have the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Which lists them in order of decreasing ionic radius?

options.text: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
O²⁻ = F⁻ = Na⁺ = Mg²⁺
Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻
Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > O²⁻ > F⁻

questions.explanation: Same 10 electrons, so size depends on nuclear charge: 8, 9, 11 and 12 protons. More protons pull the same electrons closer, so radius decreases from O²⁻ to Mg²⁺.

questions.stem: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom emits the photon of highest frequency?
questions.explanation: Falls to n = 1 cross the biggest gaps, because levels are widest apart near n = 1. Highest energy, highest frequency.

questions.stem: The first ionisation energy of magnesium is lower than that of beryllium. Which explains this?

options.text: Magnesium has more electrons, so the nucleus's pull is shared among more of them.
Magnesium's outer electron is in shell 3, further from the nucleus and more shielded.
Magnesium's 3s electrons are paired, and their repulsion makes one easy to remove.
Magnesium is more reactive, so it gives up its outer electron more readily.

questions.explanation: Mg is [Ne] 3s², Be is 1s² 2s². The extra shell adds distance and shielding, which outweigh the larger nuclear charge (+12 against +4), so less energy is needed.

questions.stem: What is the maximum total number of electrons that the first three main energy levels of an atom (n = 1, 2 and 3) can hold?
Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine. Which explains this?

options.text: A fluorine atom has more protons than a chlorine atom, so it pulls harder on a shared pair.
Fluorine needs only one electron to fill its outer shell, so it attracts electrons strongly.
In fluorine the shared pair is closer to the nucleus and shielded by fewer inner electrons.
Fluorine releases more energy than chlorine when it gains an electron, so it is more electronegative.

questions.explanation: Fluorine's bonding electrons are in shell 2, shielded only by 1s². Chlorine's are in shell 3, shielded by 10 inner electrons. Shorter distance and less shielding outweigh chlorine's larger nuclear charge.

questions.stem: Lithium compounds give a crimson-red flame. Sodium compounds give a yellow-orange flame. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Lithium's electrons fall across a larger energy gap, because red light has the longer wavelength.
The flame is hotter around sodium, so the same transitions give out higher-energy light.
Sodium's excited electrons fall across a larger energy gap, so each photon has more energy.
Sodium's electrons give out yellow photons as the flame raises them to higher levels.

questions.stem: Why does silicon have the highest melting point of the Period 3 elements?

options.text: It is a giant covalent lattice, so melting breaks many strong covalent bonds.
Its Si₂ molecules have the strongest London forces in the period.
It has four delocalised electrons per atom, so its metallic bonding is the strongest.
Its atoms have the most electrons in the period, so the forces between them are the strongest.

questions.explanation: Each Si atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant lattice. All those strong bonds must be broken, which needs far more energy than overcoming London forces or the metallic bonding in Al.

questions.stem: An argon atom has seven more electrons than a sodium atom, yet argon's first ionisation energy is about three times sodium's. Which explains this?

options.text: Argon's outer shell is full, and a full shell is stable, so it does not want to lose an electron.
Argon has more electrons, so the extra electron–electron repulsion holds its outer electron in place.
Argon's outer electron is in a higher shell than sodium's, so it is held more tightly.
Argon has 18 protons to sodium's 11, and its outer electrons are in the same shell with similar shielding.
